## Paragraph 1

**Original** — parse 0/4 · connectives 4 · terms 1 · continuity 1/3 · cost 374 (83 words)

> Grammar decisions need a tie-breaker. Our research findings (docs/research/cnl-design-findings.md) ground sentence difficulty in measurable cognitive load: peak simultaneously-open dependencies (comfortable ceiling ≈4), dependency length, and center-embedding depth predict "hard to mentally unpack" better than any stylistic rule. They also showed categorical structural bans overshoot — a heavily left-branching sentence was effortless when it carried little load — so the right constraints are load bounds, not shape prohibitions. Human readers and LLMs share the relevant profile: both integrate left-to-right under a bounded working context.

- (rejected, ×1) The first criterion is the load. Prefer the structure that keeps the Open Dependencies small, keeps the Dependency Length short, and keeps the Embedding Depth shallow. The branching rules exist to help the reader and the Language Model, so the rules follow the results of the science of cognition, not the taste of the writer. The second criterion is the common construction. When the ideal structure is unavailable, choose the frequent pattern of standard English, because the familiarity helps the reader and the surprise costs the reader. The third criterion is the small Context Need. A sentence must work with a small amount of prior context, so the language bans Anaphoric Pronouns, repeats the nouns, and fixes the scope rules. The fourth criterion is the density inside the bounds. The target is a precise text that is dense in meaning but cheap to process, so prefer the short formulation that stays inside the load bounds. The verbosity adds noise, and noise creates a reading ambiguity. The rules that force extra words are justified only if the rules remove more ambiguity than the added length costs. The fifth criterion is the expressiveness. Angloform must be pleasant to read, but the expressiveness does not override the 4 criteria above. The corollaries are 2 rules. The first rule states the constraints as bounds, not as bans on shapes. The second rule states that a long formulation must earn the trade, because the length is cheap but never free. The enforcement hierarchy has 2 tools. The primary tool is the set of valid Sentence Shapes, because the Grammar makes the bad shapes unwritable. The secondary tool is the scoring of the Parses, because the scoring monitors the residual load and gathers the evidence. Every future ADR must justify the choice against the 5 criteria, in the order of the criteria. The metrics for the first criterion exist in the results of the research, and the metrics can run over the output of the Parse.

- (rejected, ×1) Load is the first criterion. Prefer the structure that minimizes the Open Dependencies, the Dependency Length, and the Embedding Depth. The branching rules exist to help the reader and the Language Model, so the rules follow the results of the cognitive science, not the taste of the writer. The second criterion is the common construction. When the ideal structure is unavailable, choose the frequent pattern of standard English, because the familiarity helps the reader and the surprise costs the reader. The third criterion is the small Context Need. A sentence must be interpretable with a small amount of prior context, so the language bans Anaphoric Pronouns, repeats the nouns, and fixes the scope rules. The fourth criterion is the density inside the bounds. The target is a precise text that is dense in meaning but cheap to process, so prefer the short formulation that stays inside the load bounds. The verbosity adds noise, and noise creates a reading ambiguity. The rules that force extra words are justified only if the rules remove more ambiguity than the added length costs. The fifth criterion is the expressiveness. Angloform must be pleasant to read, but the expressiveness does not override criteria 1 through 4. The corollaries are 2 rules. The first rule states the constraints as bounds, not as bans on shapes. The second rule states that a long formulation must earn the trade, because the length is cheap but never free. The enforcement hierarchy has 2 tools. The primary tool is the set of valid Sentence Shapes, because the Grammar makes the bad shapes unwritable. The secondary tool is the scoring of the Parses, because the scoring monitors the residual load and gathers the evidence. Every future ADR must justify the choice against these 5 criteria, in this order. The metrics for the first criterion exist in the research results, and the metrics can run over the Parse output.

- (rejected, ×2) The criteria for every syntactic-structure decision rank in this order. Cognitive load is first. The structure must minimize the open dependencies, the dependency length, and the embedding depth. The branching rules help a human reader and help a Language Model, because the cognitive-science results ground the rules. The rules do not follow a taste or a tradition. The fallback is the most common construction. If the ideal branching is not available, then the writer chooses the most frequent pattern of standard English. The familiarity helps the reader, and the surprise costs the reader. The context need is minimal. A sentence must need as little prior context as possible. The language bans every Anaphoric Pronoun, repeats every noun, and fixes every scope rule, so the context need is small. The density stays inside the bounds. The target is a dense text that is cheap to process. The writer prefers the shortest formulation that stays inside the load bounds. Verbosity is not free. A verbose text adds noise, and the noise creates a Scope Ambiguity. A rule that forces extra words is justified, because the rule removes more ambiguity than the added length costs. A rule that pads without disambiguating fails this criterion. The expressiveness is subordinate. The text must sound natural, charismatic, and expressive. An angloform sentence must be pleasant to read. The expressiveness does not override criteria 1 through 4. If 2 valid formulations tie on the load, on the density, and on the context need, then the writer prefers the more expressive one. The writer never trades precision or clarity for charisma. The corollaries follow. The constraints are bounds. A bound limits the weight of the fronted material. The constraints are not a ban on shapes. If a rule forces a longer text, then the trade must earn the length. The length is cheaper than the load. The length is not free. The enforcement hierarchy follows. The primary tool is the set of valid Sentence Shapes. The comprehension properties are built into the Grammar, so the bad shapes are not writable. The scoring of the parsed sentences is the secondary tool. The scoring verifies the claim, monitors the residual load, and gathers the evidence for future bounds. The scoring is not the mechanism that keeps the text readable. Every future Grammar ADR must justify the choice against these 3 criteria, in this order. The metrics for criterion 1 already exist in the research findings. The metrics can implement over the parse output when the Grammar tier arrives. The natural sounding text loses to the measurably easier text when the 2 conflict. Criterion 2 keeps the loss small.

## Paragraph 5

**Original** — parse 0/3 · connectives 2 · terms 0 · continuity 0/2 · cost 144 (36 words)

> Minimal context need. A sentence should be interpretable with as little prior context as possible. This is why anaphora is banned (ADR 0002), why nouns are repeated, and why scope rules are fixed rather than context-dependent.

**Best** — parse 4/4 · connectives 2 · terms 3 · continuity 2/3 · cost 164 (51 words) · drops: none

> The Context Need of a sentence is the prior text of the sentence. A good sentence has a small Context Need. The language bans every Anaphoric Pronoun, so the writer repeats every noun. The language fixes the rules of the scope, so the reader does not depend on the prior context.

> Density within the bounds. The target is precise, meaning-dense text that is nonetheless cheap to process: prefer the shortest formulation that stays inside the load bounds. Verbosity is not free — text that under-compresses its meaning adds noise, and noise creates its own reading ambiguity. Rules that force extra words (repeated nouns, mandatory then) are justified only because they remove more ambiguity than the added length costs; a rule that pads without disambiguating fails this criterion.

> Enforcement hierarchy: the primary tool is the set of valid sentence structures — comprehension properties (notably right-branching, which the head-initial templates make structurally inevitable) are built into the grammar, so bad shapes are unwritable rather than merely penalized.
